name: Verner's Law
statement: Grimm's law's exceptions dissolve once you know where the ancient word-accent fell.
meaning: Verner's law explains a class of apparent exceptions to Grimm's law in the history of the Germanic languages. Grimm's law had turned certain Proto-Indo-European voiceless consonants into voiceless fricatives, but in some words the expected sound came out voiced instead, seemingly at random. Verner showed the difference was not random: the fricative became voiced when the original Indo-European word-accent did not fall on the immediately preceding syllable.
mechanism: The conditioning factor is the position of the old Proto-Indo-European word-accent, which could fall on different syllables and is still visible in cognates in Sanskrit and Greek. When that accent sat on the immediately preceding syllable, the fricative stayed voiceless and Grimm's law held; when it fell elsewhere, the fricative, and inherited s as well, turned voiced. Germanic later shifted all stress onto the root or first syllable, erasing the accent that had done the conditioning, so the outcomes looked arbitrary until Verner compared them against the older accent preserved in Sanskrit.

examples.text: Sanskrit shows the accent on the root in the word for brother but on the ending in the word for father; correspondingly Germanic keeps a voiceless fricative in brother but has a voiced one in father.
The law produces consonant alternations within a single verb's forms, the grammatischer Wechsel, as in the s-to-r alternation surviving in English was versus were.
Words that looked like counterexamples to Grimm's law fell into line once the accent condition was applied, turning apparent chaos into regularity.

variants.name: Grammatischer Wechsel
variants.text: The systematic voiced-voiceless alternation within the forms of one word, a direct fingerprint of the law, arising because the accent shifted across a word's inflected parts in Indo-European.

variants.name: Rhotacism
variants.text: The later change by which the voiced s that Verner's law produced often became r, as in the was-were and lose-forlorn alternations of English.

whyItMatters: It was a landmark for the Neogrammarian principle that sound changes are exceptionless once the right conditioning is found. By showing that Grimm's law's exceptions were themselves perfectly regular, governed by an accent no longer visible in Germanic, Verner's law vindicated the young science of historical linguistics and its faith in regular sound laws, and it remains a textbook demonstration of how apparent irregularity can hide a deeper rule.

working.text: when a Germanic reflex seems to break Grimm's law, check where the Proto-Indo-European accent fell, using Sanskrit or Greek cognates.
predict a voiced fricative when the original accent was not on the immediately preceding syllable, voiceless when it was.
treat grammatischer Wechsel within a word's forms as a record of the ancient shifting accent, not as noise.

limits: It is a well-established, uncontroversial regular sound law of historical linguistics; what remains debated is fine chronology, including whether Verner's law strictly followed Grimm's law or interacted with it differently. Its scope covers not only the fricatives produced by Grimm's law but also inherited s, which became voiced z and often later r. Its conditioning is the ancient Indo-European mobile accent, not the fixed root-stress of later Germanic, whose shift is precisely what obscured the pattern.
misreadings: The conditioning accent is the old Proto-Indo-European one preserved in Sanskrit, not the later fixed Germanic stress; the Germanic stress shift hid the rule rather than causing it. The law is not limited to the consonants Grimm's law produced; it also voiced inherited s. And it is not a set of exceptions to be memorised but a regular law that rescued Grimm's law by explaining its apparent failures.
origin: Formulated by the Danish linguist Karl Verner, who set it out in 1875 in 'Eine Ausnahme der ersten Lautverschiebung' (An Exception to the First Sound Shift), published in 1876; it decisively supported the Neogrammarian view of exceptionless sound laws.

Verner's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the voicing of non-initial fricatives after an unaccented syllable.
